title: Noticing good things (gratitude)
keyIdea: Gratitude means noticing good things, big and small, and the people who made them happen. Even a bad day has some good bits. Gratitude does not mean pretending: you can be sad and glad at the same time. A specific thank-you says what someone did and how it helped.
familyTip: At bedtime, take turns to name three good things from the day, including one small thing and one person who made something good happen. On a hard day, name the hard feeling first, then look for one good thing together.

visual.caption: Is it a real, specific thank-you or a vague one? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Thank you for helping me with my sums
Thanks for letting me join your game
Thank you for packing my lunch

lab.caption: Flagship lab: fill a good things jar from a mixed day, match good things to people, sort big and small, be sad and glad, and write specific thanks.

kid: Gratitude means noticing good things and feeling glad about them. They can be big, like a birthday, or small, like warm socks or a friend's smile.
Most good things have a person behind them. Dad packed your lunch. Leo let you join his game. Noticing the person, and telling them, is part of gratitude.
Gratitude is not pretending. If you lost a match, you can say: I am sad we lost, and I am glad Ava cheered me up. Both feelings are real.
A good thank-you is specific. Say what the person did and how it helped: Thank you for helping with my sums. Now I can do column adding.
adult: Ages 8 to 9. The PSHE Association Programme of Study for Key Stage 2 covers the everyday things that affect feelings and simple ways to look after mental health. The DfE guidance for Relationships and Health Education (2019) asks pupils to learn simple self-care and that there is a varied range of emotions. Noticing good things is one of the NHS Five Ways to Wellbeing: take notice.

In studies by Emmons and McCullough (2003), and by Froh and colleagues (2008) with young teenagers, people who wrote down good things each week felt a little better about their lives. The gains were small but real. Treat it as a helpful habit, not a cure. A child who is often low still needs a grown-up to talk to.

Common mistakes: thinking only big things count; using gratitude to brush away a real feeling (be grateful, so stop crying), which tells a child their sadness is wrong; noticing things but not the people behind them; and quick, vague thanks. Be careful not to make gratitude a chore or a punishment.

In the lab your child picks three good things from a mixed day and matches four good things to the people who made them happen. They sort big and small good things, choose honest sad-and-glad answers for three hard moments, and build two specific thank-you notes.

practice.prompt: You write 3 good things every night for {n} nights. How many good things have you written?
practice.hint: Each night adds 3. Count in threes, {n} times.
practice.explain: 3 good things × {n} nights = {=3*n} good things to look back on.

practice.prompt: Your family wants 10 good things in the jar today. You have {n} so far. How many more do you need?
practice.hint: Count on from {n} to 10. Small things count too.
practice.explain: From {n} to 10 is {=10-n} more good things. Warm socks and a smile both count.

practice.prompt: Which of these counts as a good thing to notice?
choices: All of them: a party, warm socks and a smile
practice.hint: Do good things have to be big?
practice.explain: Big and small good things all count. Small ones happen every day.

practice.prompt: You lost the football match. Which answer is honest and grateful?
choices: I am sad we lost, and glad Ava cheered me up
I am not sad at all, everything is great
Nothing good ever happens to me
practice.hint: Can you be sad and glad at the same time?
practice.explain: Name the real feeling and notice one good thing. Gratitude does not mean pretending.

practice.prompt: Which thank-you is the most specific?
choices: Thank you for helping me with my sums
practice.hint: Which one says exactly what the person did?
practice.explain: Specific thanks name what someone did, so they know what mattered to you.

pool.prompt: Your lunch was in your bag. Who made that happen?
choices: Someone packed it, and others grew and sold the food
pool.hint: Think of every person between the farm and your bag.
pool.explain: Good things rarely just appear. Many people helped make your lunch.

pool.prompt: Mia's hamster died. Her friend says: Be grateful, at least you had him. Stop crying. What was the slip?
choices: Using gratitude to push away a real sad feeling
pool.hint: Is Mia allowed to be sad?
pool.explain: Mia can miss him and be glad they had him. Gratitude sits beside sadness; it does not cancel it.

pool.prompt: What did researchers find when people wrote down good things each week?
choices: They felt a bit better about their lives
pool.hint: The effect was real, but was it magic?
pool.explain: Studies found small but real gains in mood. It helps, but it is not a cure.

pool.prompt: Four people each name 3 good things at dinner, and you add {n} more. How many good things is that?
pool.hint: 4 people × 3 things first, then add yours.

pool.prompt: Which is a small, everyday good thing?
choices: A friend saved you a seat
pool.hint: Which one could happen on any normal day?
pool.explain: A saved seat is small and everyday. Small things happen often, so they are worth noticing.

pool.prompt: The bus driver gets you home safe. What could you do?
choices: Say thank you as you get off
pool.hint: Does doing a job mean they did not help you?
pool.explain: People doing their jobs still help you. A quick thank you notices them.

pool.prompt: Finish the note to Leo: Thank you for letting me join your game. ...
choices: I felt happy, not left out
pool.hint: Say how his kindness helped you or made you feel.
pool.explain: Saying how it helped shows Leo his kindness mattered.

pool.prompt: On a bad day you notice {n} bad things and 1 good thing. How many things did you notice?
pool.hint: Add the bad things and the good thing.
pool.explain: {n} bad things and 1 good thing make {=n+1}. The bad things are real, and so is the good one.

pool.prompt: Sam says: I can only be grateful if my day was perfect. Is he right?
choices: No, even a hard day has good bits to notice
Yes, bad days have nothing good
pool.hint: Think of the day with the lost pencil.
pool.explain: Gratitude works on ordinary and hard days too. You look for the good bits.
